title.text: Your first model: baseline model, linear regression and prediction error

objects.text: How can a computer predict winding temperature from motor load and air temperature, and how do we know it is any good?

slides.notes: Welcome to the second half of the semester. Today is your first full machine learning model. We use the motor data and we predict motor winding temperature. You have spent seven weeks learning to read, clean and chart data. Now that work pays off, because a model is only as good as the rows we give it. The ideas come first, then the lab.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can explain the words feature, target variable, baseline model and prediction error using the data in front of you. You can say why some rows must be held out, in a validation set and a test set, while a model trains.

And you can train a linear regression model and a decision tree in Python and compare both with a baseline model. Nothing is submitted today. The lab prepares you for part A of the first assignment, and I explain how at the end.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from the first seven weeks. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What does data.shape tell you about a table? Take a moment.

A good answer: It gives the number of rows and then the number of columns.

Question two. Why do we clean a copy of the file and keep the original unchanged? Say it to yourself first.

What I hope you said: So we can always go back to the raw data and check what we changed.

Question three. What is a missing value, and how does pandas show it? Write a word or two down.

The short answer: It is an empty cell with no reading. pandas shows it as NaN.

Keep these three in mind, because today builds on them.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: An input column (also called an input variable or predictor) that the model reads to make a prediction. Here: load_pct and ambient_c.
The column we want to predict. Here: motor winding temperature in deg C. When the target is a class such as yes or no, it is called a label. In Class 2 we make a yes or no label from the target.
The simplest possible model, which every other model must beat. Here it predicts the mean of the training targets for every row.
For one row: actual value minus predicted value. Later slides combine many errors into one score, the MAE or the RMSE.
The training set is the rows the model learns from. The validation set is held-out data: rows kept back while the model trains, used to compare models fairly.

objects.alt: grid
flag
check
cross
lock

slides.notes:
Five terms for today, and these are the real industry names, so you will hear them again in textbooks and documentation. Think of one reading from our file. Its load_pct and ambient_c are the features, and its motor winding temperature is the target variable. If we always guessed the mean, about 71 deg C, that guess would be the baseline model.

If the real reading were two above our guess, the prediction error would be plus two. The model learns from the training set, and we judge it on the validation set, rows it never saw. Which of the five words was new to you?

title.text:
A prediction turns past readings
into a number you can act on

objects.alt: bell

objects.text: Warn before a motor winding overheats

objects.alt: calendar

objects.text: Plan maintenance before a failure, not after it

objects.alt: gear

objects.text: Choose the right cooling fan for a motor drive (the unit that powers the motor)

slides.notes:
Let us start with why anyone predicts a number. With motor readings you can do things like these. Warn before a motor winding overheats. Plan maintenance before a failure, not after it. Choose the right cooling fan for a motor drive (the unit that powers the motor). Every one of those is a decision that costs money or safety if it is wrong, and every one starts with a number we do not yet know.

That is what a model does for us: it takes readings we already have and gives a good guess for the number we want. Which of these three sounds closest to something you would do in your own field?

title.text:
A glossary you will meet again
in textbooks and documentation

rows.text: What it means in plain words

Predicts the target as an intercept plus weighted features. Simple (also called univariate): one feature. Multiple: two or more features. Multivariate regression means several targets, a different thing.
Three scores that sum up many prediction errors, in the unit of the target (MSE: unit squared).
A missing value is an empty cell (NaN). Imputation fills it, for example with the median.
Parameters (intercept, coefficients) are learned. A hyperparameter, such as max_depth, is chosen before training.
Chains preprocessing and a model, and runs them in order.

objects.text: Each term is explained again where it first matters.

slides.notes:
Before the ideas, here is a short glossary. These are the real industry names, and you will meet them again in textbooks, documentation and interviews, so we use them from the start. Linear regression is a model that predicts the target as an intercept plus weighted features. MAE, MSE and RMSE are three ways to sum up prediction errors.

A missing value is an empty cell, and imputation fills it. Parameters are learned, and a hyperparameter is chosen before training. A pipeline runs the steps in order. Each term comes back later with a picture, and gradient descent and the loss function have their own slides. Which of these have you already heard somewhere?

title.text:
Machine learning finds the rule from
examples, so nobody writes it by hand

objects.alt: Machine learning finds the rule from examples, so nobody writes it by hand

objects.text: A model is the rule the computer found.

runs.text: We do not write the rule ourselves. The computer finds it from the examples.
Every example row must include its answer, which we call the target variable.

slides.notes:
Here is the whole idea of machine learning in one picture. We give the computer examples, which are past rows that include the answer. It looks for a pattern that links the inputs to the answer. What it keeps is called the model. Then, when a new row arrives without an answer, the model produces a prediction.

Compare that with what you did in Weeks 3 and 4, where you wrote every rule yourself with if and else. Today the computer finds the rule. Our job is to give it good rows and to check its work.

title.text:
Every row is one reading: the inputs are
features and the answer is the target variable

objects.alt: Every row is one reading: the inputs are features and the answer is the target variable

objects.text: The model reads the features and predicts the target variable (yellow): motor winding temperature in deg C.

runs.text: Features (input variables): load_pct (percent of full load) and ambient_c (deg C).
record_id and equipment_id only label the row.
Record 4 is left out: its target is a missing value (NaN).

slides.notes:
Look at the table. The grey numbers on the left are the rows of the file. Each row is one reading of one motor. The columns load_pct and ambient_c tell us how hard the motor was working and how warm the air was. Those are the features, also called input variables or predictors: the things the model is allowed to see.

The last column is the target variable, motor winding temperature in deg C. It is the answer we want the model to learn to guess. The record number and the equipment label help us keep track, but they are not features today. Which column is the target?

title.text:
Before we model, we remove
the rows we cannot trust

objects.alt: Before we model, we remove the rows we cannot trust

objects.text: Our file has 91 rows. Three kinds of row cannot be used.

runs.text: record_id 1 is in row 1 and again in the last row, row 91 (yellow). Keep the first.
record_id 4 has a missing target (NaN): nothing to learn from.
record_id 9 has load_pct -5: impossible.

slides.notes:
This is the Week 6 data cleaning you already know, now with a purpose. Our file has 91 rows, and three kinds of trouble. One record number appears twice, once near the top and once in the very last row of the file, so we keep the first copy.

One row has no target, so there is no answer to learn from. And one row has a load below zero percent, which cannot happen, so it is a recording error. After removing them we keep 88 rows. One more missing value remains, in a feature column, and we deal with it later by imputation.

Notice that we clean a copy and keep the raw file safe.

title.text:
Hold out rows while the model
trains, so the evaluation is fair

objects.alt: Hold out rows while the model trains, so the evaluation is fair

objects.text: After cleaning, 88 rows remain. We cut them into three sets by equipment group.

runs.text: Held-out data are rows not used to fit the model: the validation and test sets.
Each equipment group goes into one set only.

slides.notes:
Suppose you learned ten answers by heart and I tested you on the same ten. You would look brilliant and I would learn nothing. A model is the same. So we cut the 88 clean rows into three groups. The training set, 58 rows, is what the model learns from.

The validation set, 15 rows, is held-out data that the model never trains on, and we use it to compare models. The test set, 15 rows, is also held out and stays untouched until the end of the block. We cut by equipment group, E1 to E4, then E5, then E6, so the model is judged on whole motor groups it has never met.

Why would mixing the groups give us a rosier score?

title.text:
Imputation fills a missing value with
the training median of its column

objects.alt: Imputation fills a missing value with the training median of its column

objects.text: Training medians: 62.8 percent (load_pct) and 26.1 deg C (ambient_c). Record 14 (group E2) has no ambient_c, so it gets 26.1. This is imputation (SimpleImputer).

slides.notes:
One feature value is missing, and a model cannot use a missing value. So we fill it by imputation, with the median, the middle value of that column. The important rule is where the median comes from. We find it from the training rows only, here 62.8 for load and 26.1 for ambient temperature.

We use that same number to fill missing values in the validation set too. If the validation set helped decide the fill, information would leak from the held-out data into the model, which is called data leakage, and our score would be a little too kind. The scikit-learn tool that does this is called SimpleImputer, and we meet it in the lab.

title.text:
The baseline model comes first: predict
the mean of the training targets every time

objects.alt: The baseline model comes first: predict the mean of the training targets every time

objects.text: Each dot is one training row. The dashed line is the baseline model: it predicts 71.03 deg C for every row.

runs.text: A baseline model is the simplest possible model: it predicts the mean of the training targets and ignores the features.
Every other model must beat it. If it cannot, it has learned nothing useful.

slides.notes:
Each dot is one training row. Before building anything clever, we build the simplest possible model, called the baseline model. It predicts the mean of the training targets, 71.03 deg C, for every row, whatever the load. That dashed line is the baseline model. Look at the dots: it is fine for rows near the middle and very wrong at both ends.

This matters because any model has to do better than the baseline model, or it is not worth the trouble. How large do you think its prediction error will be, on average?

title.text:
The baseline model adds the 58 training
targets and divides by 58: 71.03 deg C

objects.alt: The baseline model adds the 58 training targets and divides by 58: 71.03 deg C

rows.text: The prediction, which is the mean of the y_i.
The actual target of training row i.
How many training rows there are.
Add up the values from row 1 to row n.

objects.text: We add the 58 training targets and divide by 58. The validation set plays no part.

slides.notes:
Here is the baseline model written as a formula. The symbol y with a little hat on top means a prediction. The symbol y with a bar on top means the mean. To get it we add up the targets of all 58 training rows and divide by 58.

For our data that gives 71.03 deg C. Every row gets that same prediction. Notice that the validation set never takes part, because it is held out. Read the table row by row and check that you can say what each symbol means in our data.

title.text:
Simple linear regression fits a line through
the dots and beats the baseline model

objects.alt: Simple linear regression fits a line through the dots and beats the baseline model

objects.text: Simple (univariate) linear regression: one feature, load_pct. Each extra 1 percent of load adds 0.67 deg C.

runs.text: At zero load it starts at 31.2 deg C (the intercept).
It predicts the target as an intercept plus a weighted feature.
On the validation set its MAE is 4.30 deg C.

slides.notes:
This model is called simple linear regression, or univariate linear regression, because it has one feature. The line has two numbers. The intercept, 31.2 deg C, is where it starts at zero load. The slope, 0.67, says that each extra one percent of load adds that much to the prediction.

This is the model: a rule that stands in for the table. Give it any load and it reads off a prediction. We drew it with load alone to keep the picture simple. On the validation set its mean absolute error is about 4.30 deg C. In the lab the model also uses ambient_c, so it learns one weight for each feature.

With two or more features the model is called multiple linear regression. Multivariate strictly means several targets, so we say multiple.

title.text:
Simple linear regression has two learned numbers:
at 60 percent load it predicts 71.13 deg C

objects.alt: Simple linear regression has two learned numbers: at 60 percent load it predicts 71.13 deg C

rows.text: motor winding temperature, in deg C
The feature of the row. Here the load alone.
The intercept (bias): the prediction when x is 0.
The slope, or coefficient (weight): how much the prediction grows when x grows by 1.
0.666 deg C per percent of load

objects.text: Example: at load_pct = 60 the prediction is 31.17 + 0.666 × 60 = 71.13 deg C.

slides.notes:
The fitted red line is a formula. The prediction equals b zero plus b one times x. B zero is the intercept, the value where the line starts at zero load. B one is the slope, how much the prediction grows when the load grows by one percent.

For our data b zero is 31.17 and b one is 0.666. Try it at a load of sixty percent: 31.17 plus 0.666 times sixty gives 71.13 deg C. The computer finds b zero and b one by itself. Which load gives the largest prediction?

title.text:
The prediction error (residual) is the
actual value minus the predicted value

objects.alt: The prediction error (residual) is the actual value minus the predicted value

objects.text: Prediction error (residual) = actual value minus predicted value, for one row. The line is simple linear regression.

runs.text: Each red segment joins a dot (actual) to the line (predicted). Its length is the error size.
Positive error: the model predicted too low.
A good model leaves short segments.

slides.notes:
How do we know if a model is good?

We look at its prediction errors, also called residuals. Each red segment is the distance between an actual value and what the model predicted. That distance is the error, actual minus predicted. If the model predicted too low, the error is positive. If it predicted too high, the error is negative.

A good model leaves small errors. A poor one leaves large errors. To compare models we need one number that sums up all the errors, and two ways to do that come next.

title.text:
e = y minus y-hat: for record 5 the
baseline model is off by -4.00 deg C

objects.alt: e = y minus y-hat: for record 5 the baseline model is off by -4.00 deg C

rows.text: The prediction error (residual) of row i. Negative means the prediction was too high.
The actual target of row i.
The row number i runs from 1 up to n, the number of rows.

objects.text: Our row: record_id 5, load_pct 57.62, ambient_c 23.4. Predicted too high by 4.00 deg C, from the values shown.

slides.notes:
Here is the prediction error as a formula. For row i, the error e i equals the actual value y i minus the prediction y hat i. The small i just says which row we mean. Our example is a validation row with a clear error, record 5.

Its actual target is 67.03 deg C. The baseline model predicts 71.03. So the error is -4.00, and the sign tells us the prediction was too high. Work out the same error yourself with a calculator before you move on.

title.text:
Worked example with hypothetical numbers: four
prediction errors give MAE 2.75 and RMSE 3.5

objects.text: MAE = (2 + 3 + 0 + 6) / 4 = 2.75.  MSE = (4 + 9 + 0 + 36) / 4 = 12.25.  RMSE = square root of 12.25 = 3.5.  These four readings are hypothetical (made up, with no unit) to show the arithmetic.

slides.notes:
Here are four hypothetical readings, made up so that you can follow the arithmetic by hand. Reading four has a prediction error of minus six. If we simply averaged the errors, the plus and minus would cancel, which hides the problem. So we remove the sign. Take the absolute value of each error: two, three, zero, six.

Their mean is 2.75. That is the mean absolute error, MAE. Or square each error first: four, nine, zero, thirty-six, mean 12.25, and take the square root to get back to the original unit: 3.5. That is the root mean squared error, RMSE. Check the first one on your own page.

title.text:
Three ways to turn many errors into
one number: MAE, MSE and RMSE

objects.alt: Three ways to turn many errors into one number: MAE, MSE and RMSE

rows.text: The error with its sign removed, and the error multiplied by itself.
deg C and deg C squared
Add the values for rows 1 to n.

objects.text: MAE and RMSE are in the unit of the target. MSE is in the unit squared. Lower is better.

slides.notes:
Here are the three measures as formulas. For MAE we take the absolute value of every error, add them up and divide by n, the number of rows. For MSE we square every error, add them up and divide by n. RMSE is the square root of the MSE, which brings us back to the unit of the target.

In our lab we score on the 15 validation rows, so n is 15. MAE and RMSE are the two you will quote. Which one punishes a large error more?

title.text:
Our own validation rows: the baseline
model and simple linear regression

objects.text: Values in deg C. Linear = simple linear regression (load_pct only). Errors use the rounded values shown. Absolute errors over 15 rows add up to 222.8 (baseline, MAE = 222.8 / 15 = 14.85) and 64.4 (linear, MAE = 4.30).

slides.notes:
Now the same arithmetic on real rows. These are the first four validation rows. The baseline model predicts 71.03 for every row, so its error is the actual value minus 71.03. The simple linear regression prediction changes from row to row, because it uses the load, and its errors are much smaller.

Over all 15 validation rows, the baseline model has absolute errors that add up to 222.8. Divide by 15 and you get an MAE of 14.85 deg C. Simple linear regression gets 4.30. Multiple linear regression, which uses both features, does better still, and it comes in a few slides.

title.text:
MAE and RMSE both measure
prediction error in the target’s own unit

objects.text: MAE

runs.text: The mean of the absolute errors
Every error counts by its size
Easy to explain to a client

objects.text: RMSE

runs.text: Squares the errors, takes the mean, then the root
One large error counts for much more
Use it when large errors are costly

objects.text: Both are in deg C: "the model is off by about this many deg C".

slides.notes:
Both measures answer the question: how far off are we, on average?

MAE treats every error the same way. If one reading was off by six and another by two, they count as six and two. RMSE squares first, so the error of six counts for nine times the error of two. That makes it the stricter measure, and the right one when a large error is dangerous, such as a motor overheating.

Both are in deg C, the same unit as the target, so we can say in plain words how far off we are. RMSE is always at least as big as MAE. Which would you quote to a client?

title.text:
Gradient descent trains a model by walking
downhill on the loss, one small step at a time

objects.alt: Gradient descent trains a model by walking downhill on the loss, one small step at a time

objects.text: Training starts with a poor model and improves its parameters (here the slope) by repeating small steps.

runs.text: Loss function: how wrong the model is, as one number (here the MSE).
Gradient: the slope of the loss. It shows which way is downhill.
Learning rate: the size of each step.

slides.notes:
How does the computer train a model?

Most models learn by trial and improvement. The model starts poor, measures the loss, given by the loss function, a single number for how wrong it is, and works out which direction lowers the loss. That direction is the gradient. Then it takes a small step in that direction, and the size of the step is the learning rate.

Too big and it overshoots. Too small and it takes forever. It repeats until the loss stops falling. Picture walking down a hill in fog, feeling the slope with your feet. That method is called gradient descent. Logistic regression next week and neural networks learn this way.

title.text:
Gradient descent, part 1: the loss L
is the MSE, and dL/dw is its slope

objects.alt: Gradient descent, part 1: the loss L is the MSE, and dL/dw is its slope

rows.text: The loss: the MSE of the model y-hat = w x over n rows (x_i, y_i).
The slope parameter (no intercept, to keep it small).
Residual y_i minus w x_i. Squaring removes the sign, so both forms of L match.
How fast L changes when w changes.

objects.text: A negative slope: a bigger w lowers the loss.

slides.notes:
Here is gradient descent as formulas. The first line is the loss itself, the mean squared error you met a few slides ago. Inside the bracket I wrote predicted minus actual, which is minus the residual, and squaring removes the sign, so it is the same loss. The second line is the slope of the loss.

The tiny example uses illustrative data, x equal one, two, three and y equal two, four, six. The model is y hat equals w times x, with no intercept. At w equal zero the slope is minus 18.67, which says that a bigger w lowers the loss.

title.text:
Gradient descent, part 2:
change w a little, downhill

objects.alt: Gradient descent, part 2: change w a little, downhill

rows.text: The parameter (slope) we are improving. It starts at 0.
Replace the old w by the new value on the right.
The slope of the loss from the last slide.
The learning rate: the size of each step.
Skips these steps: it finds b0, b1 and b2 at once with a direct formula (least squares). Logistic regression (Class 2) and neural networks learn by gradient descent.

objects.text: Repeat: new w = old w minus the learning rate times the slope of the loss.

slides.notes:
This is the second formula, the update rule. The new w equals the old w minus the learning rate times the slope of the loss. If the slope of the loss is negative, we are on the downhill side, so minus a negative number makes w bigger. The learning rate eta is 0.05.

One fact to keep straight: LinearRegression in scikit-learn solves for its parameters directly with the least-squares formula, so it never walks downhill. Gradient descent reaches the same answer step by step, and it is how logistic regression and neural networks learn. Next we calculate the first step by hand.

title.text:
On a tiny illustrative example, five
steps almost reach the best slope

objects.text: Illustrative (hypothetical) data: x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 2, 4, 6, so the best w is 2. Step 1 by hand: dL/dw = (2/3) × (1 × (0 − 2) + 2 × (0 − 4) + 3 × (0 − 6)) = -18.67. New w = 0 − 0.05 × (-18.67) = 0.933.

slides.notes:
Here is the tiny illustrative example with one step worked by hand. The inputs are one, two, three and the answers are two, four, six, so the best slope is exactly two. We start the slope at zero. The slope of the loss at zero is minus 18.67.

The new w is zero minus 0.05 times minus 18.67, which is 0.933. After step two it is 1.431. After five steps it is 1.914, very close to two, and the loss has fallen to 0.035. Nobody told the computer the answer was two. In the lab, LinearRegression gets its answer with the direct formula instead.

title.text:
Multiple linear regression has three
learned parameters: b0, b1 and b2

objects.alt: Multiple linear regression has three learned parameters: b0, b1 and b2

rows.text: motor winding temperature, in deg C
The two features (input variables) of a row.
The intercept (bias): the prediction if both features were 0. Nothing runs at 0 percent load in 0 deg C air, so it is only an anchor.
The coefficients (weights) of x1 and x2.
b1 = 0.695 deg C per percent; b2 = 1.054 deg C per deg C

objects.text: LinearRegression finds b0, b1 and b2 with the direct least-squares formula (no gradient descent).

slides.notes:
This is the model you will train in the lab, multiple linear regression. It is the same idea as simple linear regression, but with two features. The prediction equals b zero plus b one times x one plus b two times x two. X one is the load in percent and x two is the ambient temperature.

After training on our rows, b zero is 1.66, b one is 0.695 and b two is 1.054. B zero is only an anchor, because nothing runs at zero load in air at zero degrees. These three numbers are the parameters the model has learned. In the lab you print them.

Each coefficient tells you how much the prediction moves for one more unit of its feature.

title.text:
What one more unit of a
feature does to the prediction

objects.text: This is multiple linear regression. Its coefficient for load_pct is not the same as the 0.666 of simple linear regression, because now the two features share the work. The start values 60 and 25 are chosen for the example.

slides.notes:
Let us use the formula. Take a reading with a load of sixty percent and an ambient temperature of twenty-five degrees. The prediction is 69.71 deg C. Now raise the load by one percent and keep the ambient temperature fixed. The prediction rises by 0.695, which is b one.

Raise the ambient temperature by one degree instead and it rises by 1.054, which is b two. Raise both and the changes add up to 1.749. That is how you read a coefficient: the change in the prediction for one more unit of that feature, with the other feature held fixed.

title.text:
A decision tree learns a short list of
yes or no questions about the features

objects.alt: A decision tree learns a short list of yes or no questions about the features

objects.text: A row follows yes or no answers down to one yellow box, a leaf node. That leaf gives the prediction.

runs.text: Each question is an internal node: a split on a feature and a threshold. The top one asks: is load_pct at most 42.9?
The prediction is the mean target of the training rows in that leaf node.

slides.notes:
A second kind of model. A decision tree asks yes or no questions about the features and sends each row down one branch until it reaches a leaf node, the yellow box at the bottom. Each question is an internal node. The first box asks whether load_pct is at most 42.9.

If yes, the row goes left. If no, it goes right. Each yellow box is a leaf node. It predicts the mean target of the training rows that ended up there during training. This small tree has only two questions on any path, so you can read it like a rule.

Which question does the tree ask first, and why do you think it picked that one?

title.text:
max_depth is the largest number
of questions a row can be asked

objects.alt: max_depth is the largest number of questions a row can be asked

objects.text: max_depth is a hyperparameter: a setting we choose before training. It limits how many questions a row meets.

runs.text: This tree has max_depth 1. The tree on the previous slide had max_depth 2.
Deeper trees can overfit (fit noise): Class 3. The lab uses max_depth 4 and random_state=17, so ties break the same way for all.

slides.notes:
The setting called max_depth is the largest number of questions a row can be asked on the way down. It is a hyperparameter, which means a setting that we choose before training. The computer does not learn it, unlike the parameters. This tree has depth one, so one question and two answers.

The earlier tree had depth two. A deeper tree asks more questions and can fit the training rows more closely, even to the point of overfitting, which means fitting noise in the training set. In the lab you use depth four, with random_state set to seventeen so that everyone gets the same tree when two questions tie.

Class 3 shows when deeper trees stop being helpful. Why would a tree that is perfect on its training set still disappoint us?

This is where we are heading. Three models, all trained on the same training set and all evaluated on the same validation set. The baseline model has a mean absolute error of 14.85 deg C. The decision tree has 4.79. Multiple linear regression has only 0.78, the best of the three.

That is a different model from simple linear regression, which scored 4.30. The RMSE tells the same story: 16.93, 6.29 and 0.92. Do not memorise these numbers. The point is that you will produce them yourself in the lab, and that a fair comparison always includes the baseline model.

title.text:
A pipeline is one container that holds the
imputer and the model, and runs them in order

objects.alt: A pipeline is one container that holds the imputer and the model, and runs them in order

objects.text: The gold frame is the pipeline: fit learns the medians, then the model; predict fills, then predicts.

slides.notes:
Before the code, two terms. An imputer is a tool that fills missing values, here with the median of the training set. A pipeline is the container around the steps: it chains preprocessing and a model, and runs them in order. Our pipeline holds two steps: first the imputer, then the model.

When we fit the pipeline, it learns the medians and then learns the model. When we predict with it, it fills any missing value first and then predicts. Why do we put the imputer inside the pipeline instead of filling the cells by hand?

title.text:
Read the workflow before you
write it: create, fit, predict, score

runs.text: imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy=
"median"
linear_model = make_pipeline(
imputer, LinearRegression())
linear_model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = linear_model.predict(X_valid)
mae = mean_absolute_error(y_valid, y_pred)

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Line 1: an imputer fills missing values.
Lines 2 and 3: a pipeline: imputer, then linear regression.
Line 4, fit (training) on X (features) and y (target): learns the median, then b0, b1, b2.
Lines 5 and 6: predict (inference), then score by the MAE.
Baseline and tree: swap in DummyRegressor or DecisionTreeRegressor.

slides.notes:
Before we leave the concepts, look at the code you will use. Create an imputer, which fills missing values. Join it with an untrained linear regression model in a pipeline. Fit the pipeline, which means train it on the training set. Predict, which is also called inference, means produce predicted targets for the validation set.

Then score the predictions by comparing them with the actual targets. The imputer is there because one training value is missing, and a model alone would stop with an error. A capital X is the table of features, and a lowercase y is the target variable. The baseline model and the tree use the same steps, with DummyRegressor or DecisionTreeRegressor as the second piece in the pipeline.

You do not need to memorise it, because the notebook explains every line.

slides.notes:
Errors are normal, and reading them is a skill. Here are the four you will most likely meet. File not found means the data file is not next to the notebook, so upload it. Key error means you spelled a column name differently from the file, so print the columns and copy the name.

Name error means you skipped a cell above, so run all cells from the top. And a value error about NaN means a missing value reached the model, so use the imputer pipeline. Read the last line of the error first. It usually tells you the answer.
